## li2024iris · ready · full-text · relevance high
**Version:** our text is arXiv **v3 (6 Apr 2025)** with the header "Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025", so it is the ICLR camera-ready. I had no v1 and cite no v1 numbers; this is recorded in Analyst notes.

**Summary:** IRIS has LLMs infer taint specifications (which code returns attacker-controlled data, which calls are dangerous), runs CodeQL with them, then has an LLM triage each reported path. On CWE-Bench-Java (120 real CVEs in Java projects) it roughly doubles CodeQL's detections, but precision stays low and the gain depends on how strong the LLM is.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1/RQ3 [V] (p. 8), moderate: IRIS+GPT-4 detects 55/120 vs CodeQL 27/120. Average false discovery rate (share of reported paths that are not the known bug, AvgFDR) is 84.82% vs 90.03%; AvgF1 0.177 vs 0.076.
- RQ1 [V] (p. 8), moderate: other SAST tools find Infer 0, SpotBugs 4, Snyk 23 of 120.
- RQ3 [V] (p. 8, 10), moderate: only GPT-4 lowers FDR below CodeQL. Llama-3 8B and DeepSeekCoder 7B have FDR around 95%, and the LLM triage step makes small models worse.
- RQ3 [V] (p. 10), moderate: ablation shows both LLM sources and sinks are needed (27 / 36 / 24 / 55).
- RQ3 [V] (p. 22–24), moderate: runtime is 43 s to 4 h per project with Llama-3 8B; dollar cost is not reported.
- RQ4 [V] (p. 8), moderate: GPT-4 vs CodeQL by CWE is CWE-94 8 vs 0, CWE-79 13 vs 4, CWE-22 31 vs 22, CWE-78 3 vs 1 (CWE-78 is hard for every tool).
- RQ2 [V] (p. 7, 19), moderate: the new benchmark CWE-Bench-Java has 120 compilable, manually vetted CVEs, average 300K lines of code.
- RQ2/RQ5 [I], weak: possible training-data contamination with public CVEs is never discussed.
- RQ5 [A] (p. 10), moderate: the authors say many vulnerabilities are still missed, the many LLM calls raise cost, and only Java was tested.

**Doubtful points:**
- IRIS runs on a CodeQL build the authors patched with an extra dataflow edge (p. 20), while the baseline is stock CodeQL. This is a possible confound.
- The "detected" criterion is lenient: any path through the patched method counts.
- There is no LLM-only or deep-learning baseline, so it says nothing direct about LLM vs DL for RQ1.
- The refined FDR estimate of 46% rests on only 50 manually checked alarms.
- The 4 "new" vulnerabilities have no reported developer confirmation.

## xiong2026sifting · ready · full-text · relevance high
**Version:** arXiv v3 (23 Jul 2026), formatted as the published ISSTA 2026 article (PACMSE), accepted 2026-06-25.

**Summary:** Three LLM agent frameworks (Aider, OpenHands, SWE-agent) with three backbones (Claude Sonnet 4, DeepSeek Chat, GPT-5) are tested as false-positive filters on SAST output. Data: OWASP Benchmark, 50 real-world Java CodeQL alerts (Vul4J), and 50 C/C++ alerts from after the model's training cutoff (OSS-Fuzz). The best agent removes most of the noise but also hides a sizeable share of real vulnerabilities, and results depend strongly on the backbone model and the CWE.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1 [V] (p. 11), moderate: SAST alone on OWASP: CodeQL precision 60.3%, recall 97.0%, false-positive rate 68.2%; Semgrep FPR 74.8%; SonarQube FPR 94.6%; Joern recall 8.2%.
- RQ3 [V] (p. 12), moderate: the union of SAST tools has an FPR of 98.3%. After filtering it is 6.3% with SWE-agent+Claude, vs 23.0% for plain (non-agent) Claude prompting.
- RQ3 [V] (p. 18), moderate: the same best configuration wrongly filters 22.25% of true vulnerabilities (314 of 1,411).
- RQ3 [V] (p. 12), moderate: plain DeepSeek prompting (11.2%) beats every DeepSeek agent (13.1–15.8%).
- RQ3 [V] (p. 17), moderate: cost is $0.0028–$0.1867 and 11k–269k tokens per alert.
- RQ1/RQ3 [V] (p. 13), weak: on real-world Java, agents identify up to 93.3% of false positives; best F1 is 83.3%.
- RQ3/RQ5 [I] (p. 13), weak: derived from Table 4 percentages, the GPT-5 configurations filter out about 47–67% of the true vulnerabilities on real-world Java. The authors do not discuss this.
- RQ2/RQ3 [V] (p. 15), weak: on the post-cutoff C/C++ set, SWE-agent F1 is 95.5% vs plain prompting 51.6% and an LLM4SA-style prompt 70.8%. Giving plain prompting the same files the agent opened does not help (F1 51.6%).
- RQ4 [V] (p. 18), moderate: injection CWEs are filtered reliably (true vulnerabilities missed ≤2.38%); crypto and policy CWEs badly (missed 50–84.5%).
- RQ5 [A] (p. 19), moderate: the authors say agents are unsuitable for automatic suppression and should support human review.

**Doubtful points:**
- The abstract says the initial FP rate was "over 92%", but the results give 98.3%.
- Table 3 reductions look like percentage-point drops but are described as "% of FPs eliminated".
- Two different Zenodo DOIs are given for the artifact.
- No significance tests, even though the abstract says "significantly".
- Incomplete runs are silently dropped in Table 4 (denominators below 50).
- In the ablation, removing config-file access gives a higher score than the full agent (F1 97.7% vs 95.5%), which shows how noisy N=50 is.

## du2026reducing · ready · full-text · relevance medium
**Version:** arXiv **v1 (26 Jan 2026)** with a placeholder "Conference'17" header. This is not the ICSE-SEIP camera-ready that metadata records.

**Scope:** these are **general static-analysis bugs, not security vulnerabilities**: Null Pointer Dereference (NPD), Out-of-Bounds (OOB) and Divide-by-Zero (DBZ), reported by Tencent's in-house quality analyser BkCheck, mostly on C/C++ code. The paper calls them "memory safety bugs" and maps none of them to CWEs. They overlap CWE-476/125/787/369 (my reading), so this is indirect evidence for our topic; this is stated at the top of the analysis.

**Summary:** On 433 industrial alarms (328 false, 105 real), methods that combine static analysis with an LLM beat LLM prompting alone and off-the-shelf deep-learning detectors. The best one (LLM4PFA) removes 94–98% of false alarms at under $0.12 and under 1 minute per alarm.

**SAST alone vs hybrid, with exact numbers:**
- SAT alone: reports all 433 alarms; 76% are false. Precision is about 0.24 by my arithmetic from Table 1.
- LLM4PFA (hybrid) across GPT-4o / Claude-Opus-4 / Qwen-3-Coder / DeepSeek-R1:
  - Accuracy 0.93–0.94.
  - Precision 0.83–0.93 and recall 0.75–0.88, with the real bug as the positive class.
  - Share of false alarms removed (the paper's FPR_R) 0.94–0.98.
- LLM4SA (hybrid): accuracy 0.86–0.92, false alarms removed 0.84–0.96.
- Basic prompting: accuracy 0.40–0.55, false alarms removed 0.26–0.52.
- Cost per alarm: LLM4PFA takes 12.6–58.3 s and $0.0025–$0.12. Across all LLM methods it is 2.1–109.5 s and $0.0011–$0.12. Cost per project or scan is not reported.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1/RQ3 [V] (p. 6, 8), moderate: the SAT alone has 76% false alarms; LLM4PFA removes 94–98% of them while keeping 75–88% of real bugs.
- RQ3 [V] (p. 8), moderate: hybrids (accuracy 0.86–0.94) beat prompting-only LLMs (0.40–0.72).
- RQ1 [V] (p. 7–8), weak: Devign, ReGVD, LLMAO and LineVul fail at this task (accuracy 0.36–0.44; LineVul labels every alarm false).
- RQ3 [V] (p. 6, 8), moderate: the per-alarm costs above, vs 10–20 minutes for manual review.
- RQ4 [V] (p. 8–9), weak: methods do best on DBZ and worst on NPD; failures go with long functions and many conditionals.
- RQ5 [A] (p. 9–10), moderate: recall is below the 90% enterprise threshold, and LLMs can only filter alarms, not find bugs the analyser missed.
- RQ2 [I], weak: scope caveat, since these are general bugs, private C/C++ data, and the winning method is the authors' own.

**Doubtful points:**
- Conflict of interest: LLM4PFA is the authors' own earlier tool, evaluated on private data that cannot be checked.
- The deep-learning comparison is unfair: vulnerability detectors (and one fault-localisation model) were used without retraining for alarm triage.
- Model names in the text do not match the references. For example, "Claude-Opus-4" cites Claude 3.5 Sonnet and "DeepSeek-R1" cites DeepSeek-Coder-V2, so the exact model versions are uncertain.
- Neither the ">90% FP rate when counting excluded records" figure nor the "explanations cut review from 10 to 3 min" claim has a described measurement.
- The analysis header lists only 6 of the 9 authors because the scaffold truncated it; metadata itself is complete and I did not edit it.

The best agent removes most of the noise but also hides a sizeable share of real vulnerabilities, and results depend strongly on the backbone model and the CWE.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1 [V] (p. 11), moderate: SAST alone on OWASP: CodeQL precision 60.3%, recall 97.0%, false-positive rate 68.2%; Semgrep FPR 74.8%; SonarQube FPR 94.6%; Joern recall 8.2%.
- RQ3 [V] (p. 12), moderate: the union of SAST tools has an FPR of 98.3%. After filtering it is 6.3% with SWE-agent+Claude, vs 23.0% for plain (non-agent) Claude prompting.
- RQ3 [V] (p. 18), moderate: the same best configuration wrongly filters 22.25% of true vulnerabilities (314 of 1,411).
- RQ3 [V] (p. 12), moderate: plain DeepSeek prompting (11.2%) beats every DeepSeek agent (13.1–15.8%).
- RQ3 [V] (p. 17), moderate: cost is $0.0028–$0.1867 and 11k–269k tokens per alert.
- RQ1/RQ3 [V] (p. 13), weak: on real-world Java, agents identify up to 93.3% of false positives; best F1 is 83.3%.
- RQ3/RQ5 [I] (p. 13), weak: derived from Table 4 percentages, the GPT-5 configurations filter out about 47–67% of the true vulnerabilities on real-world Java. The authors do not discuss this.
- RQ2/RQ3 [V] (p. 15), weak: on the post-cutoff C/C++ set, SWE-agent F1 is 95.5% vs plain prompting 51.6% and an LLM4SA-style prompt 70.8%. Giving plain prompting the same files the agent opened does not help (F1 51.6%).
- RQ4 [V] (p. 18), moderate: injection CWEs are filtered reliably (true vulnerabilities missed ≤2.38%); crypto and policy CWEs badly (missed 50–84.5%).
- RQ5 [A] (p. 19), moderate: the authors say agents are unsuitable for automatic suppression and should support human review.

**Doubtful points:**
- The abstract says the initial FP rate was "over 92%", but the results give 98.3%.
- Table 3 reductions look like percentage-point drops but are described as "% of FPs eliminated".
- Two different Zenodo DOIs are given for the artifact.
- No significance tests, even though the abstract says "significantly".
- Incomplete runs are silently dropped in Table 4 (denominators below 50).
- In the ablation, removing config-file access gives a higher score than the full agent (F1 97.7% vs 95.5%), which shows how noisy N=50 is.

## du2026reducing · ready · full-text · relevance medium
**Version:** arXiv **v1 (26 Jan 2026)** with a placeholder "Conference'17" header. This is not the ICSE-SEIP camera-ready that metadata records.

**Scope:** these are **general static-analysis bugs, not security vulnerabilities**: Null Pointer Dereference (NPD), Out-of-Bounds (OOB) and Divide-by-Zero (DBZ), reported by Tencent's in-house quality analyser BkCheck, mostly on C/C++ code. The paper calls them "memory safety bugs" and maps none of them to CWEs. They overlap CWE-476/125/787/369 (my reading), so this is indirect evidence for our topic; this is stated at the top of the analysis.

**Summary:** On 433 industrial alarms (328 false, 105 real), methods that combine static analysis with an LLM beat LLM prompting alone and off-the-shelf deep-learning detectors. The best one (LLM4PFA) removes 94–98% of false alarms at under $0.12 and under 1 minute per alarm.

**SAST alone vs hybrid, with exact numbers:**
- SAT alone: reports all 433 alarms; 76% are false. Precision is about 0.24 by my arithmetic from Table 1.
- LLM4PFA (hybrid) across GPT-4o / Claude-Opus-4 / Qwen-3-Coder / DeepSeek-R1:
  - Accuracy 0.93–0.94.
  - Precision 0.83–0.93 and recall 0.75–0.88, with the real bug as the positive class.
  - Share of false alarms removed (the paper's FPR_R) 0.94–0.98.
- LLM4SA (hybrid): accuracy 0.86–0.92, false alarms removed 0.84–0.96.
- Basic prompting: accuracy 0.40–0.55, false alarms removed 0.26–0.52.
- Cost per alarm: LLM4PFA takes 12.6–58.3 s and $0.0025–$0.12. Across all LLM methods it is 2.1–109.5 s and $0.0011–$0.12. Cost per project or scan is not reported.

**Evidence rows:**
- RQ1/RQ3 [V] (p. 6, 8), moderate: the SAT alone has 76% false alarms; LLM4PFA removes 94–98% of them while keeping 75–88% of real bugs.
- RQ3 [V] (p. 8), moderate: hybrids (accuracy 0.86–0.94) beat prompting-only LLMs (0.40–0.72).
- RQ1 [V] (p. 7–8), weak: Devign, ReGVD, LLMAO and LineVul fail at this task (accuracy 0.36–0.44; LineVul labels every alarm false).
- RQ3 [V] (p. 6, 8), moderate: the per-alarm costs above, vs 10–20 minutes for manual review.
- RQ4 [V] (p. 8–9), weak: methods do best on DBZ and worst on NPD; failures go with long functions and many conditionals.
- RQ5 [A] (p. 9–10), moderate: recall is below the 90% enterprise threshold, and LLMs can only filter alarms, not find bugs the analyser missed.
- RQ2 [I], weak: scope caveat, since these are general bugs, private C/C++ data, and the winning method is the authors' own.

**Doubtful points:**
- Conflict of interest: LLM4PFA is the authors' own earlier tool, evaluated on private data that cannot be checked.
- The deep-learning comparison is unfair: vulnerability detectors (and one fault-localisation model) were used without retraining for alarm triage.
- Model names in the text do not match the references. For example, "Claude-Opus-4" cites Claude 3.5 Sonnet and "DeepSeek-R1" cites DeepSeek-Coder-V2, so the exact model versions are uncertain.
- Neither the ">90% FP rate when counting excluded records" figure nor the "explanations cut review from 10 to 3 min" claim has a described measurement.
